traditions/oneness-pentecostal/summary: A branch of Pentecostalism that arose from the 'New Issue' at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting (1913), when teachers such as R. E. McAlister and Frank Ewart urged baptism 'in the name of Jesus' only. It teaches that God is one person who manifests as Father, Son and Spirit, rejecting the doctrine of three persons and so standing outside historic Nicene orthodoxy (its adherents see it as restoring apostolic faith). Major bodies include the United Pentecostal Church International (1945), and Oneness churches are strong in Latin America, Ethiopia and China (the True Jesus Church).
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/distincti: God as one being and one person, revealed in Jesus
Baptism in the name of Jesus only
New birth as repentance, Jesus-name baptism and Spirit baptism with tongues
Holiness standards of dress and conduct in many churches
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/profile/a: Scripture as the inspired Word of God, with emphasis on Acts 2:38 as the pattern of salvation.
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/profile/s: Repentance, water baptism in Jesus' name and receiving the Holy Spirit with tongues together constitute the new birth.
Ordinances of Jesus-name baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and often footwashing.
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/profile/g: Varied; the UPCI has district and general conferences with congregational local churches.
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/profile/w: Pentecostal worship with tongues, healing and exuberant praise.
traditions/oneness-pentecostal/status: Active; estimates range from c. 20 to 30 million adherents worldwide; outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/summary: The spread of Pentecostal-style experience of the Holy Spirit within historic churches, beginning publicly when Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett announced his Spirit baptism in Van Nuys, California (1960). It spread through Lutheran, Presbyterian, Anglican and Orthodox circles, and from the Duquesne Weekend (1967) into Catholicism, where the Catholic Charismatic Renewal received papal encouragement. Charismatics generally remained in their denominations, integrating gifts of the Spirit with their own theology and sacramental life.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/distincti: Baptism in (or release of) the Spirit within existing churches
traditions/charismatic-renewal/profile/a: Each participant's church tradition (Scripture, creeds, magisterium) combined with openness to the Spirit's present activity.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/profile/s: Follows the host tradition's soteriology; Spirit baptism understood as renewal of grace already received (e.g. in baptism and confirmation).
As in the host tradition; Catholic charismatics retain the seven sacraments.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/profile/g: Renewal networks and service committees within existing church structures.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/profile/w: Prayer meetings with praise, tongues, prophecy and healing alongside traditional liturgies.
traditions/charismatic-renewal/status: Active; c. 305 million charismatics in 2010 (Pew), the majority Catholic.
traditions/neo-charismatic/summary: A broad 'third wave' category for independent and post-denominational churches with Pentecostal-charismatic spirituality that are neither classical Pentecostal nor part of renewal in historic churches. It includes the Vineyard movement (John Wimber), networks such as Hillsong and Bethel, many Nigerian, Brazilian and Korean megachurches, and the New Apostolic Reformation associated with C. Peter Wagner. Some streams emphasise power evangelism, apostolic networks or the prosperity gospel, which other Christians strongly criticise.
traditions/neo-charismatic/distinctives/: Apostolic and prophetic leadership in some streams
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/autho: Scripture, with strong openness to present-day prophetic words and apostolic leadership.
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/salva: Evangelical faith in Christ, with expectation of healing, deliverance and empowerment.
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/sacra: Believer's baptism and communion, usually as ordinances.
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/escha: Varied; some hold dominion or 'kingdom now' views, others classical premillennialism.
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/gover: Often founder-led or apostolic networks rather than denominations.
traditions/neo-charismatic/profile/worsh: Extended contemporary worship sets, ministry times with prayer for healing and prophecy.
traditions/neo-charismatic/status: Active; among the fastest-growing Christian groups (hundreds of millions by WCD's broad definitions).
traditions/african-initiated-churches/su: Churches founded by Africans rather than by missionaries, beginning with 'Ethiopian' churches that broke from mission control in the 1880s–1890s, such as Mangena Mokone's Ethiopian Church in Pretoria (1892). Prophet-healing movements followed: the Harrist churches (West Africa, 1913), the Kimbanguist church (Congo, 1921), Aladura churches in Nigeria, and Zionist and Apostolic churches in southern Africa, including the Zion Christian Church. They integrate African cultural forms with the Bible, emphasising healing, prophecy and protection from evil.
traditions/african-initiated-churches/di: Use of holy water, robes and sacred sites
Attention to dreams, visions and spiritual protection
Some practise polygamy-tolerant or Old Testament-influenced customs
traditions/african-initiated-churches/pr: Scripture, often read alongside the revelations of prophet-founders and the guidance of the Spirit.
Salvation in Christ understood holistically: forgiveness, healing, protection and well-being.
Baptism (often by immersion in rivers), communion and many healing rituals.
Varied; some expect a new Jerusalem centred on holy cities such as Moria or Nkamba.
Often led by prophet-founders and their successors, with bishops or archbishops.
Vibrant worship with drums, dance, prayer for healing and white robes.
The Protestant canon; some churches add founders' hymns or writings.
traditions/african-initiated-churches/st: Active; tens of millions of members (estimates often exceed 60 million).
traditions/chinese-house-churches/summar: Unregistered Protestant congregations in the People's Republic of China that refused to join the state-sanctioned Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954). Drawing on indigenous movements such as Watchman Nee's Little Flock and Wang Mingdao's independent church, they survived the Cultural Revolution in secret and grew dramatically from the late 1970s, especially in rural Henan and Anhui and later among urban professionals. They have faced recurrent crackdowns, including the closure of Chengdu's Early Rain Covenant Church in 2018.
traditions/chinese-house-churches/distin: Theology shaped by persecution and suffering
Indigenous Chinese hymnody (e.g. the Canaan Hymns)
traditions/chinese-house-churches/profil: Scripture as the supreme authority, interpreted largely through evangelical and indigenous Chinese traditions.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with strong emphasis on conversion and holy living.
Baptism (often of believers) and the Lord's Supper.
Often premillennial; some networks promote the 'Back to Jerusalem' missionary vision.
Independent congregations and large rural networks; urban churches increasingly Reformed or presbyterian.
Small home gatherings with prayer, Bible study and singing.
traditions/chinese-house-churches/status: Active; estimates of membership range widely, from c. 30 million to over 60 million.
traditions/latter-day-saints/name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
traditions/latter-day-saints/summary: Founded by Joseph Smith in 1830 in New York state, it emerged from the same restorationist milieu as the Stone–Campbell movement, teaching that the true church had been lost in a 'Great Apostasy' and restored through new revelation. Its scriptures include the Book of Mormon alongside the Bible. After Smith's death (1844) most members followed Brigham Young to Utah. Its doctrine of God, which describes the Father, Son and Holy Ghost as three distinct beings, places it outside historic Nicene orthodoxy, although members regard themselves as Christians.
traditions/latter-day-saints/distinctive: Restoration of priesthood authority and prophetic leadership
Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price as scripture
Temple ordinances, including eternal marriage and baptism for the dead
Extensive lay ministry and missionary service
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/aut: The Bible 'as far as it is translated correctly', the Book of Mormon and other modern scriptures, and continuing revelation through living prophets and apostles.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/sal: Salvation through the atonement of Jesus Christ, received by faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost and enduring to the end; exaltation requires temple covenants.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/sac: Ordinances: baptism by immersion at age eight or older, confirmation, the weekly sacrament (bread and water) and temple ordinances.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/esc: Christ's Second Coming and millennial reign, resurrection, and a final judgment assigning people to degrees of glory.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/gov: Hierarchical: President (prophet), First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles; lay bishops lead wards.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/wor: Sunday sacrament meetings in chapels; temple worship for members in good standing.
traditions/latter-day-saints/profile/can: The Bible (King James Version in English), Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price.
traditions/latter-day-saints/status: Active; c. 17.5 million members (2024); outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/summary: A movement that grew from the Bible Student circles of Charles Taze Russell, who was influenced by Adventist thinkers and began publishing Zion's Watch Tower in 1879. Under Joseph Rutherford it adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses (1931). Witnesses teach that Jehovah alone is almighty God, that Jesus is God's first creation and that the Holy Spirit is God's active force, positions outside historic Nicene orthodoxy. Known for door-to-door evangelism, refusal of blood transfusions and political neutrality, Witnesses have faced persecution, including in Nazi Germany and modern Russia.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/distinctiv: Use of the divine name Jehovah
Jesus as God's first creation; denial of the Trinity
Refusal of blood transfusions, military service and political involvement
Expectation of Armageddon and an earthly paradise
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/au: The Bible (New World Translation) as interpreted by the Governing Body, regarded as the 'faithful and discreet slave'.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/sa: Salvation through faith in Christ's ransom sacrifice and faithful obedience; 144,000 anointed go to heaven, while a 'great crowd' inherits paradise on earth.
Baptism by immersion as a symbol of dedication, and an annual Memorial of Christ's death (partaken only by those claiming to be anointed).
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/es: Imminent Armageddon, Christ's thousand-year reign, resurrection to a restored earth and annihilation of the wicked; no hellfire.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/go: Centralised under the Governing Body; congregations led by appointed elders and ministerial servants.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/wo: Meetings in Kingdom Halls for Bible study, instruction and song; no clergy class.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/profile/ca: The 66-book canon in the New World Translation.
traditions/jehovahs-witnesses/status: Active; c. 8.8 million active publishers (2023); outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
traditions/lutheran/summary: Churches shaped by Martin Luther's reformation and the confessions gathered in the Book of Concord (1580), above all the Augsburg Confession (1530). Lutherans understand themselves as a reform movement within the catholic church, centred on justification by grace through faith for Christ's sake. Once dominant in Germany and Scandinavia, Lutheranism now has its fastest growth in Ethiopia (Mekane Yesus), Tanzania, Madagascar and Indonesia. Most Lutheran churches belong to the Lutheran World Federation, which signed the Joint Declaration on Justification with Rome in 1999.
traditions/lutheran/distinctives/0: Justification by grace alone through faith alone
traditions/lutheran/distinctives/2: Real presence of Christ's body and blood 'in, with and under' the bread and wine
traditions/lutheran/distinctives/3: Theology of the cross and the two kingdoms
traditions/lutheran/distinctives/4: Rich hymnody and church music (Luther, Bach)
traditions/lutheran/profile/authority: Scripture as the sole norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions as a faithful exposition (norma normata) and the ancient creeds.
traditions/lutheran/profile/salvation: Sinners are justified by God's grace alone, received through faith alone, on account of Christ alone, apart from works; good works follow as fruits of faith.
traditions/lutheran/profile/sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, with confession/absolution sometimes counted; sacraments are means of grace in which God gives forgiveness.
traditions/lutheran/profile/eschatology: Christ's visible return, resurrection of all, judgment, eternal life and condemnation; the Augsburg Confession rejects millennial kingdoms.
traditions/lutheran/profile/governance: Varied: episcopal in Scandinavia (some with historic succession), synodal or consistorial elsewhere; historically linked to state churches.
traditions/lutheran/profile/worship: Liturgical Divine Service with Word and Sacrament following the church year, with strong congregational hymn singing.
traditions/lutheran/profile/canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha historically printed between the Testaments as useful reading.
traditions/lutheran/status: Active; c. 77 million in LWF member churches (2022), more in other Lutheran bodies.
